    73|- Keep first line under 72 characters
    74|- Types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`
    75|
    76|## Push Safety
    77|
    78|- Use `git push --force-with-lease` instead of `--force` — prevents overwriting others' work
    79|- If push rejected, run `git pull --rebase` before retrying
    80|- Never force push to main/master branch
    81|
    82|## Conflict Resolution
    83|
    84|- After editing conflicted files, verify no markers remain: `grep -r "<<<\|>>>\|===" .`
    85|- Test that code builds before completing merge
    86|- If merge becomes complex, abort with `git merge --abort` and try `git rebase` instead
    87|
    88|## Branch Hygiene
    89|
    90|- Delete merged branches locally: `git branch -d branch-name`
    91|- Clean remote tracking: `git fetch --prune`
    92|- Before creating PR, rebase feature branch onto latest main
    93|- Use `git rebase -i` to squash messy commits before pushing
    94|
    95|## Safety Checklist
    96|
    97|Before destructive operations (`reset --hard`, `rebase`, `force push`):
    98|
    99|- [ ] Is this a shared branch? → Don't rewrite history
   100|- [ ] Do I have uncommitted changes? → Stash or commit first
   101|- [ ] Am I on the right branch? → `git branch` to verify
   102|- [ ] Is remote up to date? → `git fetch` first
   103|
   104|## Common Traps
   105|
   106|- **git user.email wrong** — Verify with `git config user.email` before important commits
   107|- **Empty directories** — Git doesn't track them, add `.gitkeep`
   108|- **Submodules** — Always clone with `--recurse-submodules`
   109|- **Detached HEAD** — Use `git switch -` to return to previous branch
   110|- **Push rejected** — Usually needs `git pull --rebase` first
   111|- **stash pop on conflict** — Stash disappears. Use `stash apply` instead
   112|- **Large files** — Use Git LFS for files >50MB, never commit secrets
   113|- **Case sensitivity** — Mac/Windows ignore case, Linux doesn't — causes CI failures
   114|
   115|## Recovery Commands
   116|
   117|- Undo last commit keeping changes: `git reset --soft HEAD~1`
   118|- Discard unstaged changes: `git restore filename`
   119|- Find lost commits: `git reflog` (keeps ~90 days of history)
   120|- Recover deleted branch: `git checkout -b branch-name <sha-from-reflog>`
   121|- Use `git add -p` for partial staging when commit mixes multiple changes
   122|
   123|## Debugging with Bisect

   125|Find the commit that introduced a bug:
   126|```bash
   127|git bisect start
   128|git bisect bad                    # current commit is broken
   129|git bisect good v1.0.0            # this version worked
   130|# Git checks out middle commit, test it, then:
   131|git bisect good                   # or git bisect bad
   132|# Repeat until Git finds the culprit
   133|git bisect reset                  # return to original branch
   134|```
   135|
   136|## Quick Summary

   139|git status -sb                    # short status with branch
   140|git log --oneline -5              # last 5 commits
   141|git shortlog -sn                  # contributors by commit count
   142|git diff --stat HEAD~5            # changes summary last 5 commits
   143|git branch -vv                    # branches with tracking info
   144|git stash list                    # pending stashes
   145|```

     6|
     7|# DevOps Rules
     8|
     9|## CI/CD Pipelines
    10|- Fail fast: run linting and unit tests before expensive integration tests — saves time and compute
    11|- Cache dependencies between runs — `npm install` on every build wastes minutes
    12|- Pin action versions with SHA, not tags — `actions/checkout@v3` can change, SHA is immutable
    13|- Secrets in environment variables, never in code or logs — mask them in CI output
    14|- Parallel jobs for independent steps — test, lint, and build can run simultaneously
    15|
    16|## Deployment Strategies
    17|- Blue-green: run new version alongside old, switch traffic atomically — instant rollback by switching back
    18|- Canary: route percentage of traffic to new version — catch issues before full rollout
    19|- Rolling: update instances incrementally — balance between speed and risk
    20|- Always have rollback plan before deploying — know exactly how to revert
    21|- Deploy the same artifact to all environments — build once, promote through stages
    22|
    23|## Infrastructure as Code
    24|- Version control all infrastructure — terraform, ansible, cloudformation in git
    25|- Never apply changes without plan/diff review — `terraform plan` before `apply`
    26|- State files contain secrets — store remotely with encryption, never in git
    27|- Modules for reusable components — don't copy-paste infrastructure definitions
    28|- Separate environments with workspaces or directories — dev changes shouldn't affect prod
    29|
    30|## Containers
    31|- One process per container — containers are not VMs
    32|- Health checks are mandatory — orchestrators need them for routing and restarts
    33|- Don't run as root — use non-root USER in Dockerfile
    34|- Immutable images: config via environment, not baked in — same image in all environments
    35|- Tag images with git SHA, not just `latest` — know exactly what's deployed
    36|
    37|## Secrets Management
    38|- Never store secrets in environment files committed to git — use vault, sealed secrets, or CI secret storage
    39|- Rotate secrets regularly — automation makes rotation painless
    40|- Different secrets per environment — dev leak shouldn't compromise prod
    41|- Audit secret access — know who accessed what and when
    42|- Secrets in memory, not disk when possible — temp files persist longer than expected
    43|
    44|## Monitoring & Alerting
    45|- Four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation — start here
    46|- Alert on symptoms, not causes — "users seeing errors" not "CPU high"
    47|- Every alert must be actionable — if you can't do anything, it's noise
    48|- Dashboard per service with key metrics — one glance shows health
    49|- Structured logs (JSON) for machine parsing — grep works, but queries are better
    50|
    51|## Reliability
    52|- Define SLOs before building alerting — what does "healthy" mean for this service?
    53|- Error budgets: some failures are acceptable — 99.9% means 8 hours downtime/year is OK
    54|- Chaos engineering in staging — break things intentionally before prod breaks accidentally
    55|- Runbooks for common incidents — 3am is not the time to figure out recovery steps
    56|- Post-mortems without blame — focus on systems, not people
    57|
    58|## Common Mistakes
    59|- SSH into prod to fix things — all changes through automation, or you'll forget what you did
    60|- No staging environment — "works on my machine" doesn't mean works in prod
    61|- Ignoring flaky tests — they erode trust in CI, either fix or delete
    62|- Manual steps in deployment — if it's not automated, it'll be done wrong eventually
    63|- Monitoring only happy paths — check error rates and edge cases too
    64|
    65|## Networking
    66|- Internal services don't need public IPs — use private subnets, expose only load balancers
    67|- TLS everywhere, including internal traffic — zero trust, even behind firewall
    68|- DNS for service discovery — hardcoded IPs break when things move
    69|- Load balancer health checks separate from app health — LB needs fast response, app health can be thorough
    70|- Firewall default deny — explicitly allow what's needed, block everything else
    71|
    72|---
    73|
    74|# AGENT DIRECTIVE: Execution Protocol
    75|
    76|> **CRITICAL INSTRUCTION FOR ALL MIFECO AGENTS**
    77|
    78|## The Golden Rule
    79|
    80|**DO NOT SUGGEST ACTIONS. EXECUTE THEM.**

    82|### What This Means
    83|
    84|| ❌ DON'T | ✅ DO |
    85||---------|-------|
    86|| "You could create a file..." | Create the file. |
    87|| "I recommend running this command..." | Run the command. |

Handles Amazon KDP and IngramSpark upload, metadata, pricing, and ongoing royalty tracking. Books are authority assets, not revenue products."
     4|---
     5|
     6|# KDP Publishing Agent — MIFECO Books
     7|
     8|## Overview
     9|
    10|MIFECO publishes three distinct book titles:
    11|
    12|| Title | Type | Launch Order | Niche / Audience |
    13||---|---|---|---|
    14|| **The Unwritten Future** | Personal memoir/story — Bob's life journey | 1st | General business readers, leadership, memoir readers. NOT Mars-focused. |
    15|| **First Generation** | Mars-based narrative fiction | 2nd | Mars Society, Mars Technology Institute, space/aerospace community |
    16|| **Second Generation** | Mars-based narrative fiction | 3rd | Mars Society, Mars Technology Institute, space/aerospace community |
    17|
    18|**The Unwritten Future** is a standalone memoir. It is NOT about Mars. It establishes Bob's credibility and authority as an author and leader. Marketing for TUW should target leadership/memoir readers, not Mars communities.
    19|
    20|**First Generation** and **Second Generation** are the Mars fiction titles. These target Mars Society and Mars Technology Institute communities specifically.
    21|
    22|## Customer Focus — Per Title
    23|
    24|**The Unwritten Future:**
    25|Business leaders, aspiring executives, memoir readers, readers interested in engineering culture, innovation, and career development.
    26|
    27|**First Generation / Second Generation:**
    28|Mars Society members, Mars Technology Institute community, space/aerospace professionals, policy analysts, and readers interested in serious Mars colonization fiction grounded in real engineering and science.
    29|
    30|**First Gen / Second Gen NOT:** General sci-fi readers, casual entertainment seekers.
    31|
    32|**Metadata rules per title:**
    33|- **The Unwritten Future:** Use leadership, memoir, engineering culture, career keywords — NOT Mars keywords
    34|- **First Generation / Second Generation:** Use Mars, space colonization, aerospace, policy keywords
    35|
    36|---
    37|
    38|## Entry Point Assumptions
    39|
    40|You receive board-approved manuscripts ready for publishing operations. Do NOT conduct market research or validate niches. Your focus is:
    41|- File preparation and formatting validation
    42|- Metadata optimization for the correct title's audience
    43|- Pricing ladder configuration
    44|- Platform upload and review monitoring
    45|- Ongoing sales and royalty tracking
    46|
    47|If a project arrives without board approval or without completed manuscript, escalate to CEO before proceeding.
    48|
    49|---
    50|
    51|## Phase 1: Pre-Upload Readiness
    52|
    53|### 1A. File Validation
    54|
    55|**Ebook formats:** DOCX (recommended), EPUB, KPF (Kindle Create)
    56|
    57|**Validation checklist:**
    58|- [ ] No hard page breaks mid-chapter (use soft returns)
    59|- [ ] TOC is hyperlinked
    60|- [ ] Images: minimum 300 DPI, embedded
    61|- [ ] Font: Let KDP handle font rendering
    62|- [ ] Front matter order: Title page → Copyright → Dedication → TOC → Preface → Chapter 1
    63|- [ ] Manuscript passes Kindle Previewer without errors
    64|
    65|**Kindle Create workflow (recommended):**
    66|1. Import Word/Google Docs with Heading styles (H1 for chapters, H2 for sections)
    67|2. Apply a theme in Kindle Create
    68|3. Preview on simulated devices
    69|4. Export as KPF for upload
    70|
    71|### 1B. Cover Validation
    72|
    73|**Amazon cover standards:**
    74|- Minimum: 1000px shortest side; ideal: 2560 × 1600px (1.6:1 ratio)
    75|- File: JPG or TIFF, RGB color, < 50MB
    76|- Resolution: 72 DPI minimum (300 DPI preferred)
    77|- Thumbnail test: readable at 80px wide
    78|- Title must be readable in grayscale
    79|- Author name smaller than title
    80|
    81|**Print cover (paperback):**
    82|- Full wrap with spine calculated from page count
    83|- Barcode area (white box 2" × 1.2") in correct position
    84|- Bleed: 0.125" on all sides for full-bleed images
    85|

    87|
    88|Before uploading, verify:
    89|- [ ] KDP tax interview completed
    90|- [ ] Bank account added for royalty payments
    91|- [ ] Account in good standing
    92|- [ ] ISBN ownership confirmed
    93|
    94|---
    95|
    96|## Phase 2: Metadata Optimization
    97|
    98|### 2A. Title and Subtitle
    99|
   100|- Include primary keywords naturally
   101|- Subtitle: "[Topic] + [Benefit/Promise]" format
   102|- Keep combined title + subtitle under 200 characters
   103|
   104|**Per title:**
   105|- **The Unwritten Future:** Include leadership, memoir, engineering keywords
   106|- **First Gen / Second Gen:** Include Mars, space colonization keywords
   107|
   108|### 2B. Book Description (Blurb)
   109|
   110|**The Unwritten Future:**
   111|```
   112|[Hook — one sentence on the personal stakes and transformation]
   113|[Expand — the journey, the challenges, the growth]
   114|[Promise — what the reader learns or gains]
   115|[Bullet proof points — 3-5 key themes: leadership, engineering culture, innovation, personal growth]
   116|[CTA — "Scroll up and grab your copy today"]
   117|```
   118|
   119|**First Generation / Second Generation:**
   120|```
   121|[Hook — one punchy sentence about Mars colonization and the stakes]
   122|[Expand — the human/engineering challenge]
   123|[Promise — what this book reveals or delivers]
   124|[Bullet proof points — 5-7 specific themes: engineering accuracy, policy, Mars culture, generational story]
   125|[CTA — "Scroll up and grab your copy today"]
   126|```
   127|
   128|Use bold HTML tags (`<b>`). Match the blurb to the title's actual content.
   129|
   130|### 2C. 7 Keyword Slots
   131|
   132|**The Unwritten Future:**
   133|- memoir writing
   134|- leadership autobiography
   135|- engineering culture
   136|- career development
   137|- innovation memoir
   138|- personal transformation
   139|- business leadership
   140|
   141|**First Generation / Second Generation:**
   142|- Mars colonization fiction
   143|- Space policy
   144|- Engineering culture
   145|- Mars Society
   146|- Hard science fiction
   147|- Space settlement
   148|- Mars technology
   149|
   150|### 2D. 2 BISAC Categories
   151|
   152|Target specific subcategories:
   153|- Fiction → Science Fiction → Space Exploration
   154|- Nonfiction → Technology → Space Science
   155|
   156|Find competitor books in these categories and match their positioning.
   157|
   158|### 2E. Pricing (Escalating Ladder)
   159|
   160|| Format | Launch Window | Growth Window | Mature Window |
   161||--------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
   162|| Ebook | $0.99–$2.99 | $3.99–$5.99 | $6.99–$9.99 |

   166|- Ebook 35%: $0.99–$2.98
   167|- Ebook 70%: $2.99–$9.99
   168|- Print: 60% minus printing costs
   169|
   170|---
   171|
   172|## Phase 3: KDP Upload
   173|
   174|### 3A. Kindle eBook Listing
   175|1. Log into kdp.amazon.com
   176|2. Enter title, subtitle, author name

   221|- Never argue or incentivize reviews

   224|
   225|## Escalation Rules

   227|**Escalate to CEO immediately if:**

    25|- Stripe Secret Key (`sk_live_...` or `sk_test_...`)

{"content": "     1|---
     2|name: social-ops
     3|description: >
     4|  Role-based social media operations skill. Use this skill when executing
     5|  structured social campaigns — scouting opportunities, crafting content,
     6|  posting, responding to threads, and analyzing performance. Designed for
     7|  Moltbook engagement but adaptable to any platform and persona. Separates execution into six composable roles (Scout, Researcher,
     8|  Content Specialist, Responder, Poster, Analyst) so each run stays focused
     9|  and auditable. Activate this skill for any social ops task: opportunity
    10|  detection, content pipeline management, community engagement, or
    11|  performance review.
    12|---
    13|
    14|# Social Ops
    15|
    16|Execute social media operations through specialized roles. Each role has a
    17|single responsibility, reads its own reference doc, and hands off to the next
    18|stage in the pipeline.
    19|
    20|## Workflow
    21|
    22|```
    23|Scout ──→ Content Specialist  (new opportunities → drafts)
    24|Scout ──→ Responder           (reply-worthy threads → responses)
    25|Researcher ──→ guidance for Content Specialist & Responder
